comments.text:
Nuclear power is mainly expensive due to crippling regularory costs.  And those regulations are always moving.  A new plant that is designed to current regulatory standards, has to redesign if the regulations change before final approval.  Even after approval and after construction has started, if regulations change again they the plant needs to be modified on the fly to meet the new regulations.
That's part of the reason why there's so many plants that were cancelled partially completed (not the only reason, but a big one).
The problem with any regulation is there's a point of diminishing returns, where its costs a lot more to increase "safety" a very tiny amount.  An airplane could be made 100% safe...but it'd never get off the ground.  We accept a trade off of very, very safe, but not 100% safe... for feasibility and practicality with airplanes...otherwise we have no air travel.
We need to accept the same with Nuclear power for the same reasons.  
Not that it should be unsafe by any means, but "flawless" is the enemy of "very safe and feasible"

replies.author: @MrEstrax
replies.text: This claim reverses cause and effect. Citizens don't get affordable power by keeping capital out of the energy market; they get crushed by rate hikes when utilities have to socialize the multi-billion-dollar cost of new plants across captive residential households. Data centers act as creditworthy anchor off-takers. Look at Three Mile Island Unit 1: it shut down in 2019 because Pennsylvania refused to pass a taxpayer bailout, and merchant nuclear was bleeding cash. What brought 835 megawatts of firm, clean power back? Microsoft signing a 20-year bilateral PPA that backed a $1.6 billion private capital overhaul. Zero public rate-base risk. Furthermore, data centers are massive commercial tax anchors. In Virginia, data center equipment taxes deliver over a third of Loudoun County's entire municipal budget, taking the tax burden off local homeowners while funding public infrastructure. Large industrial power users also pay the lion's share of volumetric utility riders that fund low-income rate relief programs. Without tech balance sheets financing these high-voltage grid connections and baseload restarts, replacing retiring capacity falls directly on public utility commissions, who will hike residential kilowatt rates to pay for it.
